prize_parts.citation: for establishing the distance, driving-force and pathway dependence of long-range electron transfer through proteins

statement.case_for: Long-range electron transfer through proteins is a mechanism stated in physical terms: rates fall off with distance, depend on driving force and reorganization energy, and are controlled by the intervening medium through tunneling pathways and, later, multistep hopping. Gray and Winkler established this with time-resolved kinetics in engineered, photoinitiated metalloproteins, which made the principle quantitative and testable rather than anecdotal. It is the foundation for how respiration and photosynthesis move charge, and it has been confirmed independently for four decades. The attribution is as clean as any on this shortlist: two people, sustained joint authorship, and a defined discovery rather than a broad field. Recognition looks overdue, not early.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that this can be read as the application of Marcus theory, already honored in 1992, to proteins, and that priority is shared with Hopfield's tunneling theory and with the Dutton and Moser empirical distance rules, who are not in the credited set. It also has less visible downstream reach than a method such as C-N coupling, and my own field is close enough that I may overweight it. Only one member ranked it first, and no one else placed it in the top eight.

responses.point: Chabes ranks phase separation (B002) fourth but doubts that many cellular claims rest on more than overexpression and imaging, and says the specific cases need quantitative in vivo testing.
responses.response: I share this worry and it is part of why I place B002 below B009. A concept can be accepted while its biological attributions are uneven. Where I differ is that the credit for B002 is also spread across five names, and the three-name limit forces an explicit choice between Rosen and the Pappu and Mittag theory. I would want the expert report to say how much of the in vivo evidence holds up before the committee commits to a citation. The weakness of in vivo evidence counts against B002 at this point, but it does not decide the question for me.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Pd-catalyzed C-N coupling (B052) first: a general, ligand-controlled method used constantly in pharmaceutical synthesis, with Buchwald and Hartwig as the independent developers and Kosugi a real but non-general precedent. He calls it overdue because the 2010 prize covered C-C coupling only.
responses.response: I think this is the strongest case on the list for impact and maturity, and I would not oppose it. My reservation is procedural. Kosugi's tin-amide coupling predates the general method, and Hartwig also appears in a separate C-H functionalization entry, so the committee needs the expert report to confirm where the 1994 to 1995 priority lies before we settle on two names. If the report supports Buchwald and Hartwig, that is a clean prize. I still rank B009 higher because I weigh a mechanism that explains why charge moves through proteins above a method, even an excellent one.

responses.point: Linke, our chair, ranks phase separation first, with Hyman and Brangwynne as the identifiable 2009 P-granule discovery, and treats the omission of Rosen as a real but acceptable credit question. He is also drawn to sequencing by synthesis (B035) as a fully mature chemical invention.
responses.response: I accept that Hyman and Brangwynne are the identifiable origin of B002 and that the idea is now textbook. Where I disagree is on 'cleanest': leaving out Rosen, Pappu and Mittag is not a small matter, because the multivalency and sequence-grammar work is the physical-chemical part of the story. A two-name citation that credits the observation but not the explanation is weaker than B009, where the two people credited carried both the experiment and the framework. I do agree that B035 is mature and chemically definite, and I would keep it near the top of the discussion for a second configuration.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks C-N coupling first, calling it a game-changer that extends the 2010 cross-coupling logic, and also places PROTACs (B037) and base editing (B004) highly with the caveat that attribution in each is contested.
responses.response: I agree with his reservation about B037 and would add that I see the same difficulty in B004. The editor chemistry is elegant, but Komor, Gaudelli and Liu are all needed, and Target-AID by Nishida and Kondo is a parallel line, so a three-person limit leaves credible people out. For B037 the PROTAC concept and the cereblon mechanism are distinct achievements; combining them under one citation would require stretching the wording. I would sooner see the committee defer these until the credit is clearer than force a split now.

uncertainties: How the expert report should divide credit between Gray and Winkler's protein electron-transfer work and the Dutton and Moser distance rules, and Hopfield's earlier theory.
Whether the committee reads B009 as a new discovery or as the application of Marcus theory, and whether that is enough to be a prize on its own.
Whether the C-N coupling priority of Kosugi, Buchwald and Hartwig is as clean as the two-name proposals suggest.
How strong the in vivo evidence is for biomolecular condensates compared with the in vitro and imaging evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. Xiaodong Zou is my Stockholm University colleague and Johan Aqvist and I joined the committee together in 2015, but none of the shortlisted candidates is connected to Stockholm University or to me. Because my own research is on proton transfer and electron transfer in respiratory enzymes, I should be transparent that B009 is close to my field, which is a scientific closeness to disclose rather than a personal tie that would require recusal.
